title: Schizophrenic man 'exploded' at officers: ' ... he was bucking them off like (at) a rodeo,' psychiatric nurse testifies: FATALITY INQUIRY
article: Paranoid schizophrenic Kasim Cakmak "exploded" last May in a scene so violent that two police officers trying to take him to hospital could barely control him, a witness testified Wednesday at a fatality inquiry.
"The intensity of the outburst, I have never seen that strength ever," 16-year psychiatric nurse Mike Brohman said.
"They were trying to contain him and he was bucking them off like (at) a rodeo. I could see that they weren't able to hold him and were panicking."
Brohman called the officers to the mental health outpatient clinic at 9942 108th St. last May 11 to escort Cakmak, who had been attending a recreation program, to Alberta Hospital Edmonton.
He had been muttering to himself, following women in the building and acting so bizarrely a psychiatrist made him an involuntary patient who could be held for treatment against his will.
Brohman said the 37-year-old, 207 pound (94-kg) man "exploded" in an evacuated fourth-floor common room when he approached with the two officers.
They tried to pepper-spray Cakmak, who had a long history of mental illness. Brohman said he was hit by most of the liquid because Cakmak was flailing, kicking and "screaming like Tarzan."
It took about five minutes to force him face down on the ground, with his hands cuffed behind his back.
"The explosive outburst was unprecedented to the point where I felt ... if he would have gotten up, he would have gone through the window to the ground below."
Ninety seconds later, Brohman noticed his face was blue. Police removed the handcuffs and rolled him on to his back. There was no pulse. He had stopped breathing.
Brohman tried cardiopulmonary resuscitation before emergency workers took over.

Dr. Graeme Dowling, Alberta's chief medical examiner, testified Cakmak died of excited delirium, a rare condition affecting psychiatric patients and cocaine users in which they become so wildly agitated an overpowering adrenaline rush stops their heart.
The pepper spray probably didn't contribute to Cakmak's death, but in these cases it usually isn't effective, he said.
"That should be a warning sign to police officers that they're not just dealing with an ordinary violent patient."
Cakmak moved to Canada in 1991 from Turkey, where medical files indicate he was tortured in prison.

Robert Ergil, the president of Edmonton's Turkey Canadian Society who is representing the Cakmak family at the inquiry, said Cakmak was so frightened of uniforms he might have thought he was in danger.
He repeatedly questioned why Turkish-speaking family members weren't called to calm Cakmak, but clinic staff said this takes time and doesn't always help.
"Everybody was in danger, including Kasim, at that point," Brohman said. "When somebody is that agitated and upset, your priority is to get the patient safe first."
